t: Exactly One Consecutive Set Bits Pair — Editorial
o: We need to decide whether the binary representation of `n` contains **exactly one** occurrence of two adjacent set bits. For example, 6 = `110` has exactly one such pair (`11` at the top), so the answer is true; 5 = `101` has none, so it is false; while 7 = `111` has two overlapping pairs (`11` at positions 2–1 and 1–0), so it would be false too. Note that "exactly one" means we must both find a pair and ensure no second pair exists — merely detecting one pair is not enough. Since $n \le 10^5$ fits in 17 bits, any scan over the bits is trivially fast, so the real task is picking a clean formulation.
k: Shifting n right by one aligns every adjacent pair: n & (n >> 1) has a set bit at position i exactly when bits i and i+1 of n are both set.
The number of adjacent set-bit pairs equals popcount(n & (n >> 1)); we need this to equal exactly 1.
A value has exactly one set bit iff it is a power of two, testable in O(1) as x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0.

a.i: Convert n to its binary string (or iterate over its bits) and count positions where two consecutive characters are '1'. Return true only if that count equals exactly 1. This directly mirrors the problem statement and is the most intuitive solution.
s: Build the binary representation of n as a string.
For each index i from 0 to len-2, increment the counter when s[i] == '1' and s[i+1] == '1'.
a.t: O(log n) — we examine each of the O(log n) bits once.
a.sp: O(log n) for the binary string (Python/Java/JS); C++ uses a fixed-size bitset, i.e., O(1).

a.i: The expression n & (n >> 1) keeps bit i set exactly when both bit i and bit i+1 of n are set, so its popcount equals the number of adjacent set-bit pairs. We simply check whether this popcount equals 1. This avoids strings entirely and works on raw integers.
s: Compute x = n & (n >> 1); x marks all adjacent pairs.
Count the set bits of x using the language's built-in popcount (or a loop of x &= x - 1).
Return true iff the count is exactly 1.
a.t: O(log n) worst case for the popcount loop (O(1) with hardware/CPU popcount instructions); a handful of bitwise operations otherwise.
a.sp: O(1) — only integer variables are used.

a.i: We need n & (n >> 1) to have exactly one set bit, which is precisely the definition of a positive power of two. The classic identity x & (x - 1) == 0 tests this in constant time (with x > 0 required, since 0 also passes the identity but represents zero pairs). This gives an O(1) branch-free-style check with no loops or builtins.
a.t: O(1) — three bitwise operations and comparisons regardless of input size.

w: In an interview, start with Approach 1 to show you understand the problem, then immediately mention the shift-and-mask observation and land on Approach 3 as the optimal answer — interviewers love seeing n & (n >> 1) used to detect adjacent bits. Common pitfalls: forgetting that "exactly one" rules out inputs like 7 (`111`) or 12 (`1100`), which contain multiple pairs; and forgetting the x != 0 guard, since 0 & (0 - 1) == 0 would wrongly report true for n = 0 or n = 5. Edge cases to test: n = 0 (false), n = 3 (`11`, true), n = 6 (true), n = 7 (false), n = 12 (`1100`, false), n = 10^5 (`11000011010100000`, false). Likely follow-ups: generalize to "at least k consecutive set bits" (check (n & (n>>1) & ... & (n>>(k-1))) != 0), or handle arbitrarily large integers given as strings.
